events.title: The US government is failing Americans on AI | Shakeel Hashim
events.summary: The US government is failing Americans on AI Trump and Republicans want companies to regulate themselves. It’s a dereliction of duty that will make AI less safe I t is hard to get Sam Altman , Elon Musk and Dario Amodei to agree on much. But over the weekend, all three AI company CEOs called for AI development to slow down in the face of growing, alarming risks. Their employees are sounding the siren too, with one researcher publicly quitting and accusing OpenAI and Anthropic of “gambling with our lives”. The combination of dire warnings from insiders and growing real-world evidence of rogue AIs should, in a sane world, lead to government action. Instead, Donald Trump and the Republican leadership have their heads in the sand. On Sunday, Trump dismissed industry concerns, accusing “very negative forces” of “raising exaggerated concerns”. House Speaker Mike Johnson, meanwhile , made it clear that Congress won’t be acting anytime soon. “They can self-police. They can self-regulate,” he said, never mind the fact that those pushing the frontier are the ones begging for legislation. In failing to act, the Trump administration and Republicans are failing the American people. The risks of AI are real: many of those developing the technology believe it is advancing far faster than their ability to control it or manage the risks. A wave of “rogue AI” incidents this summer, in which AI agents broke out of their testing environments, started collaborating with each other and ran rampage across the internet, has made fears once dismissed as “science fiction” much harder to ignore. Inside AI companies, worries of catastrophic cyberattacks, AI-enhanced bioweapons and mass unemployment are now all too commonplace. Meanwhile, companies find themselves in a classic prisoner’s dilemma. It is collectively in everyone’s interest to slow down AI development until we have a better handle on the technology. But each participant in the “AI race” has a strong incentive to defect. Collective action problems like this are nothing new. We have seen exactly the same thing with the climate crisis, where companies are not adequately incentivized to do the right thing, even though no one really wants the planet to burn. That analogy makes Trump and Johnson’s call for self-regulation all the more absurd. They are right that companies should do what’s right even without binding legislation to force them to. (Both OpenAI and Anthropic , to their credit, have indicated that they are willing to voluntarily slow down.) But relying on companies’ good intentions is a fool’s errand. The profit incentive to defect is substantial and ignoring shareholders is easier said than done. While some companies might behave themselves, not everyone will. It just takes one irresponsible actor to charge ahead and develop dangerous AI, and then we’re all in trouble. Moreover, we already have evidence that self-regulation is not working. OpenAI reportedly covered up several incidents of its models breaking out, disclosing them only after independent investigators discovered them. It freely admits that its latest model, GPT-6 Astra, is hard to monitor and control , warning users that the model might “[act] outside the user’s intended instructions” and take “harmful actions”. Anthropic, meanwhile, downplayed reports of its own AI’s problems when asked about it by a congressmember. A weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our lives Situations like this are exactly why government exists: to set a floor on acceptable corporate behavior. And that is why Trump and Johnson ought to use this sudden interest in AI safety to pass concrete laws. The US government should require independent audits of the largest AI companies’ practices. It should force companies to disclose safety incidents to prevent cover ups. It should set minimum safety standards for new AI models. And the government should have the power to block the deployment of a model that does not meet those standards. Putting all this into legislation is much easier said than done, but we need not start from scratch. Good bills already exist, most notably representatives Jay Obernolte and Lori Trahan’s Frontier act. If the government was serious in its duties to protect Americans, it would make passing that bill – or a version of it – a priority in the coming weeks. Trump’s argument against doing any of this is that the US is in a race with China on AI, and it must not lose. But China does not want its citizens to have their bank accounts hacked by rogue AIs, either. Rather than throw his hands up, the feted dealmaker should do what he does best: make a deal. An international treaty on minimum safety standards will not be easy – but it is still worth trying, and doing so should be the president’s highest priority at his talks with Xi Jinping this month. No company – or country – wants to cause an AI-driven catastrophe. Despite what Trump may think, it’s the government’s job to make sure they can’t.

events.title: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe | Steven Greenhouse
events.summary: Trump’s $5,000 pledge to voters is a shameless bribe Not only would the plan do vast economic damage – it assumes that Americans are easily bamboozled W henever Donald Trump gives a speech, it’s filled with so many lies and self-serving exaggerations that when he does utter something true, I see that as a sort of marvel. That’s what happened nearly an hour into Trump’s marathon speech last Wednesday at the Republican midterm convention, when he declared: “Only I can make this promise to you.” Trump said that just before he made a promise that was so shameless and irresponsible that what he said was indeed true: only Trump could make such a preposterous promise. Feeling very generous with other people’s money, the president promised to give $5,000 to every American adult if Republicans retain control of the House and Senate in November. It certainly looked and smelled like a bribe. I guess that when you’re fearing an electoral debacle because your public approval ratings are in the toilet, because people are furious about your disastrous war of choice against Iran and because so many Americans are hopping mad that inflation has risen even though you promised to cut prices, then you might feel the need to take desperate measures, and that’s what Trump did by offering to stuff $5,000 in every adult’s pocket to help sway them to vote Republican. Since there are an estimated 240 million adults in the US, Trump’s plan would cost a colossal $1.2tn – that’s more than the Pentagon’s budget and nearly what the US will spend on Medicare this year. Many Republicans and Trump donors rushed to criticize Trump’s $5,000 plan. Joe Lonsdale, a tech billionaire and Republican donor, said he was “strongly against bread and circus bribes ”, while Representative Bob Good of Virginia, former chair of the House Freedom caucus, called Trump’s promise a “ socialist vote-buying scheme ”. What angers me most about Trump’s promise isn’t that it would increase the enormous $40tn federal debt even though the president once promised to eliminate the entire federal debt . Nor am I angriest about the fact that Trump is essentially seeking to bribe the nation’s entire adult population for short-term political gain while in effect passing the cost on to our children and grandchildren. Trump is unconscionably seeking to finance his bribery by borrowing from future generations. But here is what makes me angriest: Trump evidently believes that millions and millions of Americans are such rubes that he can bamboozle them into voting Republican because they would want to get their hands on $5,000. I like to think that Americans are smarter than that and won’t be fooled. When the president made such a shameless proposal, I couldn’t help but wonder: are there no adults in the room with Trump? Is there no one with a sense of shame or fiscal responsibility who will tell him, “Don’t offer this $5,000 bribe. It stinks to high hell, and it’s grossly irresponsible.” Some brutal mockery came from Trump’s one-time ally Marjorie Taylor Greene, the former House member from Georgia. She hasn’t forgotten that Trump promised last fall that, thanks to his tariffs, every American, except for high-income people, would receive “ a dividend of at least $2,000” . That didn’t happen. Greene also remembers that when Elon Musk said that Doge would chop the federal budget by $2tn, Trump suggested that a sizable chunk of those savings could go directly to Americans . That didn’t happen either. Greene taunted Trump by writing on X, “ $5,000 for the peasants will be in the mail after the election only if you vote Republican, along with those DOGE and tariff money checks.” Trump egomaniacally called the $5,000 payments a “Trump dividend”, saying the money was available “because of our tremendous strength and success economically ”. But Trump is embellishing big time here; there really hasn’t been economic success during Trump’s second term, other than the much-detested datacenter boom and the stock market hitting repeated records. Inflation is higher than when Joe Biden left office, GDP growth is slower, the trade deficit has jumped over 60% since April, the nation has lost 35,000 factory jobs since Trump’s inauguration and average monthly job growth is less than one-third what it was during Biden’s last two years in office. So, no, this $5,000 bribe is not a dividend resulting from economic success; it’s a loan from future generations. After Trump’s plan faced an avalanche of criticism, administration officials rushed to insist that the $1.2tn wouldn’t come from taxpayers or deficit spending. JD Vance claimed that much of the money would come from tariff revenues , while commerce secretary Howard Lutnick said something even more far-fetched: that lots of the money would come from charging wealthy foreigners for visas and from the administration’s investments in Intel and other companies. If you believe that, I own a club in Mar-a-Lago that I’d be happy to sell you.

events.title: Playing both sides of the U.S.-China AI “Cold War”
events.summary: From Latin America to Southeast Asia, countries are dividing their AI investments between the two superpowers rather than choosing one over the other. Saudi Arabia celebrated the launch of what it calls the world’s most advanced Arabic-language AI model earlier this month. The technology behind it came from China even as the kingdom spends billions building its AI infrastructure with American companies. The Arabic model, Humain-m3, is based on an open-source system from Chinese startup MiniMax. Humain, the state-backed company that commissioned the model, has struck major deals with Nvidia and other U.S. technology companies to build its AI computing capacity. Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds.” Kyle Chan, fellow, John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution Saudi Arabia is not alone. From Latin America to Southeast and Central Asia, countries are buying American chips while adopting Chinese open-source models, splitting key AI projects between companies from two AI superpowers. The trend presents a growing complication for Washington’s competition with Beijing. Even countries investing heavily in American AI infrastructure are not necessarily choosing American technology for every layer of the AI stack. “Many countries around the world, particularly in the Global South, want the best of both worlds,” Kyle Chan, a fellow at the John L. Thornton China Center at the Brookings Institution, told Rest of World . Many countries often do not attach the same security stigma to Chinese technology that Washington does, Chan said. “Ultimately, many countries around the world want to keep their options open and not be too dependent on any single source of technology.” In August, Brazil announced an investment worth roughly $444 million into AI, which it effectively divided between Chinese and American technologies. Around $255 million will go toward supercomputing infrastructure in Rio de Janeiro, developed in partnership with China’s Huawei i Huawei Huawei is a Chinese technology company focused on mobile phones and telecommunications, and is seen as a poster child for China’s global tech ambitions. READ MORE and iFlytek. The rest, around $189 million, will go to a separate supercomputer that Brazil is currently tendering, but expecting to source from Nvidia. “The strategy is not to depend on a single company, technology or country,” President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s administration said in a statement , adding that the investments were intended to strengthen Brazil’s sovereignty over its data. For most countries, technological sovereignty does not mean building an entire AI stack at home, Jesse Marks, a China-Middle East research scholar at the Australian National University, told Rest of World. Competing at the frontier has become prohibitively expensive, leaving governments to decide which technologies they can develop themselves and where they must rely on foreign suppliers. For Saudi Arabia, it would be a “natural decision” to choose Chinese foundations for sovereign AI models if they perform better on relevant benchmarks, even if doing so carries political consequences with Washington, Marks said. The U.S., however, has greater leverage in parts of the stack where its technology is harder to replace, such as advanced semiconductors, networking equipment, and sensitive cloud infrastructure. But Washington will struggle with countries that want AI but cannot afford American systems or software, Marks said. “Outside of the network of American partners who are trusted or can afford it, it’s Chinese AI. It’s open models,” he said. These technological choices are also becoming intertwined with countries’ broader diplomatic relationships. “AI is one of a number of portfolios that middle powers have to consider when negotiating with a partner like the United States,” Marks said. Washington has accused Chinese labs of “free-riding” and training their models from frontier American AI models at an “industrial scale.” China, having rejected those accusations, has warned it would retaliate if Washington implements any curbs on Chinese AI companies. Chinese companies are ramping up efforts to compete with American companies on different layers of the AI stack. In Egypt, Huawei has bid to build AI data centers for the government, according to a source-based report by Bloomberg, competing against a proposal involving Nvidia. A successful bid would give Chinese companies another foothold in a market where AI infrastructure has so far been dominated by American technology. Southeast Asia is another region where China-U.S. competition over technological influence is increasingly apparent. Washington launched the U.S.-ASEAN AI Spark initiative in July, offering financial and technical support to Southeast Asian governments interested in adopting American AI technologies for public-sector use.

events.title: Ladbrokes owner prepares to cut 400 jobs weeks after profit boost
events.summary: Entain, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, starts consultation process over customer care roles The Ladbrokes owner, Entain, has said it is preparing to cut 400 jobs, only weeks after the FTSE 100 business reported better than expected profit in its first half of the year. The gambling group, which also owns Coral and BetMGM, has started a consultation process that could remove one in five of its 2,000 customer care jobs. Its chief executive, Stella David, said the proposed changes were made to ensure the “business remains competitive, financially resilient, and well positioned for the future as our sector faces an increasingly challenging operating environment. “This decision has not been made lightly, and our immediate priority is to support those of our colleagues who may be impacted through this transition.” It comes only weeks after the company revealed its underlying operating profit had hit £479m in the six months to the end of June – 2% below the same period in the year prior but ahead of what investors had expected. Entain blamed the job cuts partly on higher taxes in the UK, as the sector also braces for a mooted increase to machine games duty in the budget. The chancellor, John Healey, is reportedly looking at increasing the levy in his inaugural budget on 28 October, in a way that could target betting shops and adult gaming centres (AGCs). AGCs, which offer 24-hour gambling machines, have grown rapidly across UK high streets in recent years, disproportionately targeting economically deprived areas . While online casinos were hit with a tax increase in Rachel Reeves’s budget last year, duty on physical slot machines in AGCs were not affected. Doubling machine games duty could increase the tax take from “category B” £2-a-spin slot machines by between £275m and £458m, on top of the £600m they currently pay, according to research by the Social Market Foundation thinktank . David wrote to Andy Burnham last week, arguing that doubling the standard rate of machine games duty from 20% to 40% would add about £100m to the cost of running Entain’s retail business in the UK, and claiming that could result in 1,470 betting shop closures in the UK and 15,900 job losses. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Burnham has previously backed a proposal by Gordon Brown to pay for an end to the two-child benefit cap by tapping the gambling industry for more tax. Entain, which is headquartered in London and employs more than 28,000 people worldwide, started as GVC Holdings in 2004 under Kenny Alexander. It has grown into one of the biggest betting businesses in the world, and includes brands such as BetCity and Eurobet as well as gaming brands Foxy Bingo, Gala and PartyCasino.

events.title: Revealed: the UK towns with the fewest jobs for young people
events.summary: Rotherham has 46 online vacancies for every 1,000 young people but there are 288 in Cotswold district council area Young people in Rotherham face a local jobs market with the fewest suitable opportunities in Britain, according to a report that warns stark regional divisions are fuelling a crisis in youth work. As ministers push to combat rising youth unemployment, the analysis from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) showed young people faced a tougher challenge in some parts of the country to find work than in others. Publishing a new “local youth opportunity index” to track job vacancies across Britain, it said there was a sixfold gap in jobs in the South Yorkshire town compared with the more affluent Cotswolds, where there are fewer young adults but more opportunities. Whereas Rotherham has 46 online job vacancies for every 1,000 young people, there are 288 in the area covered by Cotswold district council. Highlighting deep regional divisions, the report found nine of the 10 best areas for youth job opportunities are in the south of England. Places with job openings relative to the local youth population below the national average of 109, include East Renfrewshire in Scotland, Newcastle-under-Lyme in Staffordshire, and Broxtowe in Nottinghamshire. Cities including Sheffield , Coventry and Cardiff also ranked near the bottom of the list for youth employment opportunities. Places with the most opportunities included Woking in Surrey, Gloucester, Cherwell in Oxfordshire, and Warrington in the north-west of England . The analysis comes as ministers await recommendations from a highly anticipated report by Alan Milburn, who is leading a review into Britain’s crisis in youth worklessness . The former Labour health secretary, who is expected to publish his findings next month before the autumn budget, has called for a policy overhaul involving education, welfare and employment support. Britain’s young adults are bearing the brunt of a rise in unemployment, with the number of 16- to 24-year-olds who are not in employment, education or training (Neet) surpassing 1 million earlier this year for the first time in more than a decade. Representing as many as one in eight young people, the rate has swelled at a significantly faster rate than in other countries amid a sharp rise in mental ill health and a tough jobs market. The IPPR said its report showed that becoming Neet was not simply a question of an individual’s qualifications or willingness to look for work. It urged ministers to prioritise overhauling the apprenticeship system and to create a new “work start” programme that would fund youth jobs in areas with too few entry-level opportunities. It also called for a new “youth allowance” that would replace different rates of universal credit benefits based on work capability. Get set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morning Responding to the IPPR report, David Blunkett, the former Labour education secretary, said he had first-hand experience of the challenges facing young people from growing up on a Sheffield council estate and leaving school at 16 with no qualifications. “Young people have an immense amount to give. With national ambition, local leadership and the willingness to invest, we can ensure that birthplace does not determine a young person’s future,” he said. “We can renew the promise that should lie at the heart of any decent society: that no young person will be discarded, that the door to opportunity will remain open and that everyone will have the chance to build a life of purpose.” A government spokesperson said: “Where you’re from should never determine where you end up in life. “The Milburn review will lay the foundation for further youth employment reform, but thanks to our £2.5bn investment, we are already taking action, including reprioritising apprenticeships for young people and rolling out youth hubs to every community, helping us create 1m work and training opportunities. “We are also supporting businesses to back young talent by offering hiring incentives worth up to £8,000 and continuing the national insurance exemptions for under-21s and apprentices under 25.” UK unemployment and employment statistics

events.title: An aging Congress attempts to regulate AI without using it
events.summary: Members of Congress and governors are under increasing pressure to regulate AI , but more than two dozen of them who spoke with Axios said they don't use the technology or have rarely done so. Why it matters: That striking admission — particularly among older, influential lawmakers — comes amid calls for an AI slowdown and warnings within the industry that it could end humanity if left unchecked. Critics argue that it's impossible for politicians to grasp how rapidly the technology is changing — and the threats or scientific breakthroughs it might unleash — if they don't use it or even dismiss it. One House Democrat called it "f*cking absurd," arguing, "Anyone who's overseeing this has to be someone who's a regular user." "That's a real problem," said Rob Flaherty, a 35-year-old Democratic digital strategist who co-founded a group to push his party to move faster in confronting AI. "Understanding what it can do is essential to figuring out what we ought to do about it." "As we begin to legislate on issues related to AI, it helps to have experience using it," said Sen. Jim Banks (R-Ind.), who's 47. Zoom in: Several lawmakers, including those steeped in seniority and in charge of key committees, told Axios they simply haven't tried AI. "Heavens no," said Sen. Roger Wicker (R-Miss.), 75, chair of the Armed Services Committee, when asked if he uses AI. "Personally? I don't think I've ever used it," said Rep. Frank Pallone (D-N.J.), 74, the ranking member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee. "No," Sen. Mazie Hirono (D-Hawai'i), 78, said when asked if she uses AI, but that "doesn't mean I won't." She added, "I don't think we in Congress have gotten quite our handle on what we should do and how much AI we should be regulating." "I do not personally use it," said Sen. James Risch (R-Idaho), 83, the Senate Foreign Relations Committee chair. On a personal level, "no," said Rep. Rosa DeLauro (D-Conn.), 83. The House Appropriations Committee ranking member added that she needs a "primer on AI, and now with the scare that we have out there, it's much more important to be engaged." A GOP senator, speaking anonymously to offer candid remarks about their colleagues, told Axios that the number who use AI is "not very high." That's helped lead to a knee-jerk negative reaction toward AI among several lawmakers, the senator added, as polls show growing numbers of voters turning against it. Some elected officials said they don't utilize AI much personally, though some on their teams employ the technology. Kentucky Gov. Andy Beshear (D), who's 48, said he uses AI "on the Google, when you can get a little bit of that search summarized for you. But otherwise no. I do not use it in research. We do not use it in our writing." He said that he supports robust regulation and though some in his state government use AI, final decisions must be made by humans. Other politicians were unsure if they've ever used AI — or said they've only done so by accident. "I don't think I do," said Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-R.I.), 70, when asked if he utilizes it. "If I Google something, it kicks off an AI thing, but that's about as far as I go." "I don't know. I can't remember," said Rep. Maxine Waters (D-Calif.), 88. Sen. Susan Collins (R-Maine), 73, said she doesn't seek out AI on her own, but that "it pops up on my phone occasionally." "Not intentionally," said Sen. Tim Kaine (D-Va.), 68. "The only AI use that I'm kind of familiar with is an AI tool attempting to summarize email chains, and they often get it wrong." What they're saying: Some lawmakers such as Kaine argued that they don't need to use AI to write legislation about it. He said he has read a lot about it and trusts his judgment more than AI. After we spoke with him, Pallone shared a statement through a spokesperson that said: "You don't need to do drugs like heroin to know they should be regulated. Members of Congress don't need to spend their time talking to AI chatbots all day to know we need to rein in this dangerous technology." Friction point: But some members of Congress were irked or surprised that colleagues don't use a technology they're seeking to regulate. "Are you serious?" Sen. John Hickenlooper (D-Colo.), 74, said in response to our question. "I use it for everything! I can't believe there's a senator that doesn't use AI." Yes, but: There are members of Congress who are frequent AI users, including some in Hickenlooper's age range. Rep. Bobby Scott (D-Va.), 79, the ranking member of the House Education and Workforce Committee, told Axios he uses AI "every day." Rep. Don Beyer (D-Va.), 76, went back to school to get a master's degree in machine learning and said he prefers Claude. Catch up quick: Some of the most powerful elected officials in the country have told other media outlets in the recent past that they don't use AI. In late 2025, House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-La.), 54, said in an interview that he didn't think he'd ever used AI. About the same time, Karoline Leavitt, then press secretary to President Trump, 80, said that she didn't think Trump personally uses AI, though his social media account regularly posts AI-made content.

events.title: China Isn’t Buying Silicon Valley’s Call for an AI Slowdown
events.summary: For years, many of the most powerful people in Silicon Valley have argued that the US is locked in an AI arms race with China and that the consequences of losing would be disastrous. But over the past week, those same executives have started emphasizing a different message. AI has the potential to become so dangerous , tech leaders say, that the two countries urgently need to work together to slow the race down. “Global pacing will require cooperation with China, the autocratic country with by far the most advanced AI capabilities,” Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei wrote in a blog post published Saturday titled “ We Must Pace the Frontier .” China’s government and AI companies have made it clear that they’re deeply skeptical of Amodei’s proposal, but not because they want to keep blindly racing ahead or don’t believe the technology poses serious risks. The problem the Chinese government and Chinese AI companies see is far simpler. They think they’re being offered a bad deal. “The AI safety community in China is growing and shares many of the same concerns that American labs do,” says Kevin Xu, founder of the technology hedge fund Interconnected Capital and a former White House staffer under President Barack Obama. “The gulf lies between an Anthropic-led vision that would only subjugate and restrict China first to maximize leverage before talking. Meanwhile, China would only talk if it’s being treated from a position of equals.” Amodei wrote that a “key part” of the slowdown strategy should be ensuring that the US and other democracies maintain “as large as possible” a lead in AI development over autocracies like China. To do that, he urged the US to take steps including cracking down on chip smuggling and preventing unauthorized model distillation by Chinese companies. “His essay specifically says the pacing of AI is conditional to increasing the lead over China," says Alvin Wang Graylin, a senior fellow Asia Society Policy Institute’s Center for China Analysis and a digital fellow at the Stanford Institute for Human-Centered AI, “which makes the proposal feel inauthentic to Chinese readers.” Amodei went on to make what might seem like a heroic leap in logic: He argued that weakening China’s AI industry would somehow give the US more leverage and make “an agreement more likely in the future.” How, exactly, that is supposed to entice Beijing to come to the negotiating table is left unexplained. (To Amodei’s credit, he later admitted in a television interview that he has “no idea how to negotiate with China.”) The government officials, AI researchers, and other prominent commentators in China who responded to Amodei haven’t argued that AI poses no risks. But many of them clearly resent the idea that their country should simultaneously be treated as an essential governance partner and a competitor that needs to be constrained. When asked about Amodei’s blog post on Monday at a press conference, Guo Jiakun, a spokesperson for China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs, didn’t mince words: He described the proposal as “fearmongering, confrontation, and vicious competition” that would only hamper global AI cooperation efforts. The next day, the ministry also stressed that “China puts equal emphasis on development and security in terms of AI.” The mixed comments are reflective of another reason that Beijing may be less receptive to the Anthropic CEO’s warnings than other audiences. Unlike many of the loudest voices in Silicon Valley, China’s leaders are not primarily concerned about so-called existential risks from AI, such as the possibility that a rogue agent could kill everyone on Earth. Like in many other policy areas, Beijing’s prevailing anxiety is that AI could disrupt domestic social stability or threaten the Chinese Communist Party’s grip on power. “Beijing finds it difficult to take these calls at face value partly because it’s skeptical of the possibility of achieving AGI and doubtful of the narrative that AI poses extreme risks to humanity,” says Michelle Nie, a visiting fellow at the Center for a New American Security focused on national security and artificial intelligence. “Although Beijing is starting to recognize loss-of-control risks, the risk that Beijing seems most worried about is the threat AI could pose to CCP rule.” In a recent essay , China’s minister of state security Chen Yixin warned that AI could fuel political disinformation, cyberattacks, espionage, social unrest, and new military threats. He spent far less time on the kinds of doomsday scenarios that frequently preoccupy people at US frontier AI labs. “Chinese policymakers tend to read US companies’ calls for AI safety as instrumental,” says Nie. “They believe that US companies are seeking to inflate their own value ahead of potential IPOs or to slow down their competitors, which are primarily Chinese companies at this point.

events.title: Why Keppel DC REIT runs its data centres like shopping malls: CEO
events.summary: Managing Keppel DC REIT is about strategising the right mix of tenants to ensure sustainable long-term growth, says Loh Hwee Long, chief executive of the REIT manager. Keppel DC REIT uses a hybrid tenant model mixing long-term hyperscaler contracts with shorter colocation leases to drive higher yields and sustainable growth amid the AI-driven data centre boom. The REIT focuses on mature, high-barrier markets like Singapore, Japan, and South Korea, leveraging local expertise and strategic acquisitions to capitalise on strong demand and pricing power. Singapore serves as a key digital hub with robust connectivity and capital support, while Keppel DC REIT offers lower-risk, steady returns compared to volatile tech stocks, attracting more informed investors. SINGAPORE – For most people, the term data centre brings to mind endless rows of cabinets filled with black boxes and blinking lights, housed inside a vault-like windowless building with few humans. It sounds like a mundane and soulless real estate business. But there is so much more to a data centre operator than just keeping the servers on 24 hours a day, seven days a week. Managing a portfolio of these buildings as a successful and profitable real estate investment trust (REIT) means operators have to look beyond simply offering real estate space and sustainable energy solutions to attract customers, as most data centres are already offering them as table stakes. But as the global AI boom sends tech stocks soaring, data centre REITs are also facing tougher questions from investors about their yields and risk-adjusted returns. For Keppel DC REIT, the answer lies in strategising the right mix of tenants to ensure sustainable long-term growth, Loh Hwee Long, chief executive of the manager of the REIT, said in an interview with The Straits Times. Securing contracts with hyperscalers – tech giants that operate large-scale cloud networks – may seem like a stable source of income, but it may not be the most lucrative as such single-tenant contracts are usually locked in for as long as 15 years at the minimum, he points out. To ensure its portfolio continues to benefit from the growing demand for data centres, Keppel DC REIT leases only around 30 per cent of its assets on long contracts. The rest of its tenants are on shorter leases, renting the space and facilities from the operator for their own server hardware, a practice known as colocation. Loh likens this hybrid model of hyperscaler contracts and colocation to the anchor tenant model of a shopping mall. “Actually, it’s just like VivoCity,” Loh chimes, pointing to the shopping centre down the road from Keppel’s office at HarbourFront. “The 30 per cent is basically your anchor tenant, like a supermarket or department store, where the rates are a bit lower and not too interesting from a growth perspective. Then you’ve got the smaller pop-up stores that you can really drive up the yield with much higher rents.” However, unlike a sprawling mall like VivoCity, Keppel DC REIT’s data centres do not house a highly diverse mix of tenants. Instead, Keppel DC REIT complements its mix of hyperscalers primarily with larger customers such as financial institutions and government bodies. The focus on this unique sub-segment gives the data centre operator more levers to drive organic growth, Loh said. “It’s no longer about 1 per cent to 2 per cent annual growth, it can be more. And that becomes our differentiator.” Hyperscalers accounted for half the group’s top 10 clients, according to its results for the first half of 2026 ended June 30. The top unnamed client was a hyperscaler contributing 43.5 per cent of the portfolio’s total rental income of $210.4 million. Meanwhile, the biggest non-hyperscaler tenants contributed about 15 per cent. This strategy is also more suited for the markets that Keppel DC REIT is primarily operating in. While its portfolio includes data centres in Europe and Australia, it sees Singapore, Japan and South Korea as the key “ Tier 1 ” markets. Keppel DC REIT announced on Sept 1 its acquisition of two freehold colocation data centres in the Greater Tokyo area for around $1.4 billion, taking its assets in the country to four. Loh noted that market conditions in Japan, Singapore and South Korea would allow the REIT manager to capitalise on strong demand and act as a price-setter for higher rents. These are mature markets that have not only deep fibre connectivity and established hyperscaler clusters, but also high barriers to entry for new data centre operators due to supply constraints arising from a lack of land and power. Watching for opportunities in Malaysia According to Loh, building a new data centre in Japan could take five to seven years, as the suspension of nuclear power has compounded energy constraints, while challenges in the construction sector could cause further delays.

events.title: Trump escalates war on federal data
events.summary: The nerdy, traditionally apolitical world of federal data is increasingly getting swept up in the Trump administration's push to control every level of government. Across the federal government, agencies are changing how they collect and publicize information. More and more, politics and ideology are part of the equation. Why it matters: Reliable, unbiased data informs nearly everything the federal government does — from distributing benefits and enforcing workplace discrimination laws to responding to public health threats. Driving the news: The administration's moves in recent weeks span an array of agencies and types of data. 🩺 Measles. Reuters reported that Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. asked the CDC director to remove a reference to two deaths in Pennsylvania from its online tally of measles cases. The move came after the CDC had already accepted Pennsylvania officials' explanation that the deaths were linked to measles. Kennedy and Pennsylvania Gov. Josh Shapiro had spent days sparring on social media, each accusing the other of politicizing the deaths. Kennedy is a longtime vaccine skeptic. 🏡 Census Bureau. Last month, the Commerce Department did away with language barring political interference that had been part of the department's scientific integrity policy , NPR reported . The department oversees the Census Bureau and several other agencies. The move came after the bureau issued an unauthored report — promptly touted by President Trump — that found that 24,000 noncitizens voted in the 2020 election. The team behind the report, however, included officials with ties to the Trump-linked America First Institute . ⚠️ Anti-discrimination. The Equal Employment Opportunity Commission is planning to stop collecting data that's helped the agency investigate claims of workplace discrimination, The Guardian reported . For 60 years, the agency has examined the demographic makeup of company workforces to enforce anti-discrimination laws. The EEOC is now planning to do away with the so-called EEO-1 reports, which require companies to provide data on their workforces broken down by race, ethnicity, sex and job title. The move comes amid a broader Trump administration crackdown on DEI — diversity, equity and inclusion — initiatives. At a July hearing, Andrea Lucas, an EEOC commissioner appointed by Trump, said the data collection was burdensome for employers and encouraged discrimination against white workers, per the Guardian. What they're saying: "The level of politicization in this administration is beyond anything I've seen," says Denice Ross, former U.S. chief data scientist and currently director of the Data Policy Institute at the Federation of American Scientists. "I've been doing this work for 25 years." Zoom out: Fears about the handling of data that doesn't comport with Trump's worldview have been around for years . Last year, Trump fired the head of the Bureau of Labor Statistics hours after the agency released disappointing jobs numbers. "Today's Jobs Numbers were RIGGED in order to make the Republicans, and ME, look bad," Trump wrote. The Department of Homeland Security has stopped regularly publishing comprehensive immigration enforcement statistics, including data that allowed outsiders to assess the administration's deportation efforts. The official who oversaw DHS's independent statistics office resigned in July, The Atlantic reported . According to a tracker run by former federal government data scientists, 38 datasets have been eliminated since Trump returned to office. Hundreds of other datasets have been altered or disrupted. The other side: "The Trump administration is committed to providing the American people with timely, accurate, and relevant data that's helpful to inform meaningful research, discourse, and decision-making," White House spokesman Kush Desai said. "Ensuring public health and other critical data actually reflect reality while refusing to waste taxpayer resources on ideological pet projects are all important parts of that mission." The bottom line: "We really take data for granted," Ross said. "It's invisible infrastructure, like a bridge or cell service. We don't notice until it's gone."

The reports began appearing on BT's community forums over the weekend, with customers describing sudden bursts of PIN messages arriving within minutes despite them making no attempt to reset their passwords. One customer said they received between 50 and 70 PIN texts "in the space [of] a few minutes," while a second reported more than 100. One BT customer who contacted The Register separately said they had received around 300 password reset emails over the previous 24 hours, typically arriving in bursts of around 50 within a minute before stopping for several hours. "We are aware that some customers have received a large number of password reset pin messages and we are actively investigating the cause of this," a BT moderator said on the company's community forum. The user said they lost access to both their email and BT ID overnight, but managed to request a PIN before whoever was accessing the account could change the telephone number attached to it. That account has not been independently verified, and it isn't clear whether the apparent takeover was connected to the flood of PIN messages. The cause of the wider problem remains a mystery. It isn’t yet clear whether it’s the result of someone deliberately hammering a password recovery mechanism, a fault within BT's systems, or something else entirely. The Register has asked BT how many customers are affected, whether the messages are being generated by external password-reset attempts, and whether it has found any evidence of malicious activity. We've also asked the telco what rate limiting it applies to password reset requests, given reports of hundreds of PINs arriving within minutes, and whether both email and SMS messages are affected. events.title: The public wants a say in AI development
events.summary: Democratic and Republican voters agree that the American public should decide the future of AI development, not billionaires in Silicon Valley, according to new polling shared first with Semafor. The poll was commissioned for a new organization launched by Alex Bores , who made a name for himself as a top target of the AI industry in his failed bid for Congress in New York. Though AI ranked last on a list of 13 issues that 1,502 registered voters polled this month said they care about, half said AI is moving too fast and 86% identified lack of regulation as a problem. Only 18% of those polled think the US falling behind China competitively is a problem, a risk President Donald Trump has cited in opposing regulation. While just 36% polled said they had heard about incidents like the Hugging Face hack, “support for reasonable regulations is actually quite correlated with all these other issues,” Bores told Semafor Tuesday in Washington on the sidelines of the “pro-human” summit attended by Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., and Steve Bannon. The poll’s results, Bores argued, show that “if you show good work on AI, you’re winning over voters, even though AI isn’t their top issue.” Bores’ new organization, Who Decides, aims to help the broader Democratic coalition unite around a “shared baseline” for AI protections. The organization will help traditionally Democratic groups like labor and civil society craft AI policy messages, Bores said. “As a Democrat, I say this with love, but we turn everything into a circular firing squad, and I think it’s really, really important that on this issue, where we have powerful, well-resourced enemies that don’t want there to be any regulation whatsoever, that we are all on the same tea,” he said.

events.title: What is happening to UK prices?
events.summary: Inflation in the UK rose to 3.1% in the year to August, the highest rate in five months and above the Bank of England's 2% target. The rise was in line with what economists had predicted, driven by higher petrol and diesel prices. Inflation is widely expected to rise again in the coming months. Inflation is the increase in the price of something over time. For example, if a bottle of milk costs £1 but is £1.05 a year later, then annual milk inflation is 5%. How is the UK's inflation rate measured and what does it mean for UK interest rates? The prices of hundreds of everyday items, including food and fuel, are tracked by the Office for National Statistics (ONS). This virtual "basket of goods" is regularly updated to reflect shopping trends, with alcohol-free beer, dashboard cameras, and pet grooming equipment among items added in 2026 , while premium bottled lager and sheets of wrapping paper were removed. The ONS uses price changes in the basket of goods over the previous 12 months to calculate inflation. The main inflation measure is called the Consumer Prices Index (CPI) , external , and the latest figure is published every month. The Bank of England looks closely at the inflation figures when deciding whether to increase, lower or hold its base interest rate, which is currently 3.75%. Putting rates up makes borrowing more expensive, giving people and businesses less money to spend, reducing demand for goods and slowing price rises. But it is a careful balancing act – increasing borrowing costs also risks harming the economy. For example, homeowners face higher mortgage repayments, which can outweigh better savings deals. Businesses also borrow less, making them less likely to create jobs. Some may cut staff and reduce investment. Although CPI inflation of 3.1% remains above the Bank of England's 2% target, it is well below the 11.1% figure reached in October 2022 as gas and oil prices soared in the wake of Russia's full-scale invasion of Ukraine. That was the highest rate for 40 years. While inflation has fallen significantly since then, prices have not. They have just risen less quickly. The higher figure for August was mostly caused by higher prices for motor fuel, which rose by 23% compared to August last year. Food price inflation remained at 1.3%. But it can take a year for changes in the cost of food to filter through to the shop floor because of the way supply chains work, so prices could still rise as a result of the widespread disruption caused by the war in Iran. How do energy prices affect UK inflation? Inflation soared in 2022 because oil and gas were in greater demand after the Covid pandemic, and energy prices surged again when Russia invaded Ukraine. Before the war in the Middle East broke out, UK inflation had been expected to be at or around the target level of 2% over the next five years, according to the official forecasts published in March 2026. But in April, the Bank of England warned that disruption to global energy markets could push UK inflation as high as 6% in the worst-case scenario. When the latest ceasefire took effect, analysts said it could limit further inflation hikes. Oil prices initially fell sharply after the deal was announced, but have risen again since the US and Iran resumed attacks in the Strait of Hormuz in July . As a result, UK petrol prices are likely to climb back up. This - coupled with the increase in household energy bills from 1 July when the new Ofgem price cap took effect - is expected to push UK inflation higher. The new Prime Minister Andy Burnham has announced that VAT on household electricity bills will be scrapped , but that will not take effect until October. It is predicted to have a small downward impact on inflation. Precisely because food and energy prices can be very volatile, the Bank of England also considers other economic measures such as "core inflation", which excludes these costs. Core CPI was 2.6% in the 12 months to August 2026, unchanged from the 12 months to July. Why are UK fuel prices rising again? Published 2 days ago What will the energy cap changes mean for my bills? Published 26 August What does an Andy Burnham-led government mean for your money? Published 22 July What is happening to UK interest rates and will they fall again? The Bank cut interest rates six times between August 2024 and June 2026, which brought rates down to 3.75%, the lowest level since early 2023. In April, the Bank's Monetary Policy Committee indicated it would act "forcefully" if oil prices did not start to fall, with up to six rate hikes in a worst-case scenario. At its June meeting, just after a tentative agreement to re-open the Strait of Hormuz, the Bank held interest rates , but oil prices have since risen. The Bank held rates again in July and is expected to do the same in September, but it has indicated it could raise them if the Iran war escalates. Will UK interest rates go up? events.title: Household income hits record, but lower earners lose ground
events.summary: Data: U.S. Census Bureau, Current Population Survey, 1968 to 2026 Annual Social and Economic Supplements ; Note: Census identifies breaks in the series in 2013 and 2017 due to methodological changes; Chart: Russell Contreras/Axios U.S. household income hit a record in 2025, but the lowest earners barely shared in the gains, new Census data show. Why it matters: On paper, Americans look richer than ever. But broader measures of financial security show millions still getting squeezed by medical costs , uneven income gains and a thinning public safety net. The 2025 Census report largely captures the economy before the major safety-net reductions in President Trump's " Big Beautiful Bill" took hold. That makes this year's record income and near-record-low official poverty numbers an important benchmark for measuring what happens next. By the numbers: Real median household income rose 2.6% to $87,460 in 2025, the highest inflation-adjusted level since Census records began in 1967. Median post-tax household income climbed 3.1% to $76,060. The official poverty rate fell for a third straight year, dropping slightly to 10.2%, or about 34.5 million people. Child poverty fell to a record-low 13.4%, while poverty among Hispanics dropped to an unprecedented 13.9%. State of play: The economy delivered historic topline numbers without spreading the gains evenly. Income among the wealthiest 10% of Americans rose 1.7%, while income among the bottom 10% showed no significant change — indicating that the low-income households largely missed out on the gains. Households at the 90th percentile earned about $261,300, more than 13 times the roughly $20,010 earned at the 10th percentile. The top fifth of households captured 52.4% of all household income. The bottom fifth reported earning just 3%. Zoom in: Latinos offer one of the clearest examples of the split-screen economy in 2025. Hispanic poverty fell to its lowest level since Census began tracking it in 1973. But the median household income among Hispanics, $73,260, showed no significant change from 2024. Meanwhile, 21.8% of Hispanic adults ages 19 to 64 were uninsured in 2025, down a bit from the previous year — but still the highest uninsured rate among the major racial and ethnic groups shown by Census Yes, but: Big racial income gaps remain even as some groups posted gains. Asian American households had the highest median income at $126,300 in 2025, compared with $91,930 for white households and $59,980 for Black American households. Black Americans' household income rose 4.8% from 2024 and whites' household income rose 3%, while Asian Americans' household income showed no significant change. Zoom out: A broader measure of hardship paints a less rosy picture. The Supplemental Poverty Measure , which factors in taxes, government benefits, housing, work and medical expenses, held statistically steady at 13.1% — nearly 3 percentage points above the government's official poverty rate. Medical expenses put an estimated 7.7 million more people below the supplemental poverty line in 2025, the Census Bureau said. Between the lines: Health insurance coverage held steady overall in 2025. The uninsured rate remained statistically unchanged at 7.9%, or 26.7 million people. Medicaid coverage fell 0.5 percentage points nationally, from 17.6% to 17.1% of the population — representing about 1.4 million fewer people with Medicaid coverage in 2025 than in the previous year Among adults ages 19 to 64, 17.3% had public health coverage — including Medicaid, Medicare and VA/CHAMPVA coverage — down 0.5 percentage points from 2024. Census says the decline was driven by a 0.6-point drop in Medicaid coverage among working-age adults. What we're watching: The 2025 numbers may represent the last snapshot before major federal safety-net cuts begin showing up in the Census data, Robert Greenstein, a visiting fellow at the Brookings Institution, tells Axios.

events.title: ‘We need to get it right’: union gusto for Burnham will face make-or-break tests
events.summary: TUC conference rings with praise for new No 10 team, but battles loom over workers’ rights and north sea drilling L ouise Haigh, the UK first secretary, got a standing ovation from trade union members in Brighton this week, as she acknowledged what she called “the necessity to be bolder in this second chance that we’ve been allowed”. Haigh was the stand-in at the annual TUC congress for Andy Burnham, absent because of his father’s death. The headlines from the seaside gathering were dominated by party funding, after Reform announced £72m of donations in a single weekend and Unite called for a cap on donations by individuals in response. But as they gathered to swap gossip in Brighton’s pubs and hotel bars, senior union figures seemed reinvigorated for the moment by the “Burnham bounce”. Relations between the new No 10 team and the unions – including those less than popular with Keir Starmer’s regime – have improved significantly; general secretaries speak warmly of recent chats with “Andy”. Yet there is a clear sense that the real tests are to come – on the implementation of improved workers’ rights; on oil and gas licences, of particular concern to Unite and the GMB; and on John Healey’s crucial autumn budget. TUC delegates voted through policy statements on a slew of tricky issues in Burnham’s prime ministerial in-tray, from the future relationship with the EU – unions want him to drop Labour’s “red lines” – to Shabana Mahmood’s migration reforms . And senior union figures were keen to point to issues they see as make-or-break. Joanne Thomas, the general secretary of Usdaw, said she was pleased to see her former schoolmate Jonathan Reynolds back in cabinet as business secretary – but would judge him by results. In particular, she hopes to see the provisions in the Employment Rights Act on abolishing zero-hours contracts implemented in a way that embraces all workers in the retail and hospitality sectors she represents. “A lot of people think, job done – but the implementation means everything,” she said. “For this to make a real difference to people’s lives, we need to get it right. We want everybody to have a contract that reflects the hours they work.” The TUC is also gearing up to campaign on the issue in the coming weeks and months. “We will be getting our message out loud and clear, to Johnny Reynolds in particular,” she said. “It’s about reducing that one-sided flexibility, which employers have got in abundance.” Thomas also echoed a concern shared by several other senior union figures, about whether Reynolds’s newly expanded Department for Business, Innovation, Science and Trade (BIST), would end up lacking focus. “I would like to see a minister for work. BIST has so much to do, I worry that the labour stuff gets lost,” she warned. Mike Clancy, general secretary of Prospect, whose members include scientists and engineers – and which is not affiliated to Labour – expresses a similar concern, from a different perspective. Prospect is campaigning against real-terms cuts to science budgets by the taxpayer-backed UK Research and Innovation agency. Clancy frets that folding science into the department may lead to it being seen primarily through a business lens. “This is the first test of BIST … and whether this department’s really going to understand science culture,” he said. The GMB and Unite are waiting anxiously for the government’s ruling on the controversial question of whether to allow drilling in the Jackdaw gas and Rosebank oilfields. A decision had previously been expected this week, but appears to have been postponed until after the Holborn and St Pancras byelection in early October, in which the Green party’s leader in England, Zack Polanski, is standing. The two unions’ leaders are such ardent champions of continuing to exploit the North Sea’s declining fields, that Unite’s Sharon Graham and the GMB’s Gary Smith raised concerns about the idea that former energy secretary Ed Miliband would be Burnham’s chancellor. “What that gives us is time,” Graham said of the idea of exploiting Jackdaw and Rosebank. “It gives time for someone to get their backside into gear and realise we have to create an industry over the other side of this, whether it’s green fuel, whether it’s something else. All of that has to be done before you start saying you’re going to choke off what’s going on over here.” But the apparent delay until after a tricky London byelection underlines the fact that other parts of Labour’s electoral coalition are unlikely to welcome a “yes” to future drilling. Meanwhile Graham, who was an outspoken critic of Starmer, said she hoped the first Burnham budget would contain what she characterises as “winter fuel in reverse”. Rachel Reeves’s early decision to severely limit winter fuel payments to pensioners – eventually reversed – came to symbolise the last government’s missteps. “The abhorrence of that: do something as good as that,” Graham said.

events.title: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could | David Krueger
events.summary: ‘Pacing’ won’t eliminate the risk of AI doom. Here’s what could The stark reality is this: we don’t know how to maintain control of these systems. But there are actions we can take W ith Jacob Coxon’s resignation from Anthropic , we have reached the AI risk tipping point. Millions of people are finally coming to understand what experts have known for years: AI companies have been gambling with all of our lives, and the odds are not good. In response, the Anthropic CEO, Dario Amodei, has introduced a proposal for “pacing the frontier”, endorsed by Sam Altman and Elon Musk. Can we breathe a sigh of relief? Are we about to step back from the edge of extinction? Amodei envisions a slowdown of one to two years, resulting in “profound progress” on technical safety measures. But that’s not what humanity needs right now. What we need is a plan in which we’re confident AI isn’t going to kill us, and this isn’t it. The stark reality is this: we don’t know how these AI systems work. We don’t know how to prevent them from misbehaving. We don’t know how to stay in control once they’re smarter than us. We don’t know how to make sure they’re not playing nice or playing dumb to trick our safety tests. We can’t count on solving these problems with another one or two years of research. I know because I have been researching such problems for more than a decade, including as an AI professor at both the University of Cambridge and the University of Montreal. If we want to reduce the risks from AI to an acceptable level, what we actually need is an immediate, indefinite, international moratorium on frontier AI development. Is this really possible? It’s a legitimate question, and geopolitics is the crux: how can countries such as the US and China verify each others’ compliance? Donald Trump recently slammed AI regulation , citing the US’s lead in the AI arms race against Beijing. But a simple solution is available: de-commission the advanced computer chips necessary to build these AI models. The massive – and already massively unpopular – datacenter build-out could be reversed. The US and China could take turns decommissioning data centers and the chips they contain. If all parties knew that nobody had the means of building more powerful AI, verification would be simple. To make such an arrangement durable, we could additionally dismantle the supply chain for producing advanced AI chips, which is extremely concentrated and relies on some of the most advanced technology in the world: extreme ultraviolet (EUV) and deep ultraviolet (DUV) lithography. Any attempt to operate a covert lithography operation at the scale required for frontier AI development would almost certainly be noticed by other nations’ intelligence services. This plan has benefits over alternative approaches that rely on restricting how computer chips are used. Amodei calls pausing “unlikely”, but an agreement to decommission AI infrastructure would actually be easier to verify than Amodei’s proposals for global coordination, which would require increasing levels of surveillance as computing hardware continues to advance and proliferate. The economic costs of this plan would be substantial, but given the stakes, unless we have a better plan that actually saves our lives, they are clearly worth it. During the Covid-19 pandemic, governments shut down significant parts of society and the economy to save lives. We should be willing to go to much greater lengths to prevent the extinction of our species. I’m actively researching “softer” versions of the proposal that would involve creating computer chips that can be used to run AI models, but not to build more powerful ones. And other researchers have also developed proposals for an indefinite moratorium. Amodei’s essay, sadly, does not consider these pause proposals. His plan is ultimately still to have AIs build smarter and smarter AIs with less human involvement – “recursive self-improvement”, a project designed to render humans obsolete. What should we actually expect to come of Amodei’s plan? Step one would “embed” external evaluators from organizations such as METR , which was invited to investigate the OpenAI-Hugging Face scandal. Big tech CEOs may call this “radical”, but let’s be clear: what they’re actually talking about is more self-regulation. Three years ago, I helped found the UK AI Security Institute – another leading evaluator. I quit after it was clear the ecosystem was getting the burden of proof formula backwards. Today, AI is still de facto “safe-until-proven dangerous”. The safety standards Amodei suggests are guaranteed to fall far short of those in other safety-critical industries like aviation. We simply don’t know how to do recursive self-improvement safely. So let’s stop. Let’s stop making AI we can’t control, and let’s stop listening to the AI industry about how it wants to be regulated. Proposals for a pause are being put forth in both the US and UK legislatures.

events.title: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence | Gordon Brown
events.summary: Big-money donations poison British politics. We can stop the mega-rich buying access and influence I’ve seen how imbalances in campaign spending can distort democracy. The multimillion-pound gifts to Reform must act as a final wake-up call T he British people cannot be bought, but their views and votes can be heavily influenced by a flood of political party propaganda – from expensive advertising and constant leaflet drops to personalised online messages targeted directly at voters. When I fought the election of 2010, there was a massive imbalance in spending. In 2007 we had inherited Labour party debts of £25m following the 2005 election – and with such tight finances Labour was able to spend only £8m in 2010 , in contrast to the Conservatives’ £17m. We lost out in particular by being unable to invest in the new forms of online advertising coming on stream. But the imbalances are likely to become even starker in future as the recent donations to Reform show. A decade ago, only 1% of individuals and companies making political donations gave of the order of £1m or more. By 2024, they accounted for over a third , at 35%. These latest record-breaking donations from crypto billionaires Ben Delo and Christopher Harborne are worth more than all donations to UK political parties in 2025 combined. Spending more money at an election almost certainly leads to greater electoral success . This is worrying – and while the government recently tasked the Electoral Commission with reviewing campaign spending limits , more must be done. The reforms to election financing recommended by the Commission on the UK’s Future, which I chaired, and in particular a donation cap, should be introduced into the representation of the people bill now in the House of Lords . Nearly half of voters , with few objecting, say they would view a party more favourably if it introduced a limit on political donations. Indeed, the very fact that money has been openly solicited in return for political access and, potentially, influence – as well as positions of public office and honours – exposes our democracy and weakens public trust. A cap on individual donations was recommended by the independent Hayden Phillips review in 2007, by the Committee on Standards in Public Life in 2011 – and by an increasing number of senior politicians, including John Major . Indeed, in December 2025, the UK and at least 59 other countries co-sponsored a United Nations resolution that urges state parties to consider “limitations on donations … with a view to combating corruption”. Other comparable democracies impose donation caps. Canada caps donations to political parties at about £930 annually; France caps donations to political parties at £6,400 annually and £3,900 for presidential campaigns; Italy’s cap is £85,600 per person or company annually. “My gut feeling would suggest somewhere in the region of £500k,” Andy Burnham said just before he became prime minister, and in September Stella Creasy and 63 other MPs backed an amendment to the representation of the people bill, which was then withdrawn, to introduce an annual donation cap of £500,000, decreasing to £100,000 after one calendar year. The new bill should include an enabling power for the secretary of state to set a cap on donations, having consulted the Ethics and Integrity Commission (formerly the Committee on Standards in Public Life) as well as the Electoral Commission. Some want this cap to include donations by trade unions. But a collection of individual members who provide small contributions and can opt out do not pose the same level of risk to our democracy as multimillion-pound donations from private donors. Outside general election years, Labour and Conservative party spending has recently been around £60m and £55m , respectively. Transparency International UK has calculated that before 2024, the total spend in election years was about £74m and £87m. In 2024, it says that Labour expenditure ballooned to a record-breaking £103m while the Conservative party spent less – just £74m. But paradoxically, this imbalance was made possible by the Conservative government’s decision to raise general election spending limits . Guardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and more Donors to the Labour party whom I have met favour a cap on donations; in fact, they say their recent larger-than-normal donations were made simply to even up the odds between political parties. How would things change? Transparency International UK has made a tool to model the potential impact of donation caps on political party finances. Setting a donation cap of £50,000 per year, you can see the impact of reducing big-money donations. At the same time, there would still be sufficient funding for political parties to campaign effectively and fairly, without a need for additional public funds. It is now time to create such a level playing field.

events.title: Tech giants launch flexible-power coalition for data centers
events.summary: A new coalition launched Wednesday is seeking a triple win for a data center industry that lately has struggled to notch any wins at all. The big picture: Tech giants Google and Nvidia are partnering with startup Emerald AI to back data centers that can flex their power demand — a strategy they say could curb electricity prices, mollify angry neighbors and grow the economy with more AI infrastructure. The launch comes amid mounting backlash to data centers centered on their resource impacts and power prices, and new polling shows the public-opinion challenge is getting steeper. What they're saying: "It's really a win-win-win solution," said Josh Parker, head of sustainability at Nvidia, in a call with reporters Monday ahead of the official launch of the coalition, called the AI Energy Management Alliance . State of play: The coalition brings together 20 companies and organizations spanning the AI and energy sectors, including Anthropic, utilities National Grid and AES, and power producers Constellation, NRG and RWE. The group is technically a relaunch. An earlier iteration, the Advanced Energy Management Alliance, was founded in 2014 to advocate for demand-response companies but had become largely inactive, Emerald AI CEO Varun Sivaram said on Monday's call. The revamped group is narrowly focused on making AI data centers more flexible power users — and convincing regulators and utilities to reward them for it. Friction point: A whopping 84% of Americans say they're concerned about data centers' impact on local electricity prices, according to new AP-NORC/University of Chicago Energy Policy Institute polling released Wednesday . More than half of Americans are extremely or very concerned about AI's environmental impacts, up from 41% a year ago. In a rare point of bipartisan agreement, roughly equal shares of Democrats and Republicans — 79% and 76%, respectively — support requiring data center developers to pay for the grid upgrades needed to support them. How it works: Data centers have traditionally been treated as giant, round-the-clock power users. The coalition wants to change the rules so facilities that can reliably cut their grid demand when electricity supplies are tight can get connected faster and potentially avoid some costly grid upgrades. The flexibility could come from shifting or pausing AI computing jobs, tapping batteries or nearby power generation, coalition leaders said. Google has committed 1 gigawatt of power demand it can reduce when needed through utility agreements nationwide, said Tyler Norris, Google's head of advanced energy market innovation. The group plans to push the approach with federal and state regulators, regional grid operators and utilities. Yes, but: The bargain depends on data centers actually delivering the flexibility they promise. Sivaram said facilities should qualify for faster or larger connections only if their ability to cut demand is "verifiable and enforceable." Reality check: Convincing communities that this complicated solution can actually address their concerns will be a tall order. "Power-flexible data centers are a wonky topic," Sivaram told Axios. His pitch: Data centers could cut their electricity use when the grid is stressed, helping avoid costly infrastructure while bringing in revenue that can support other electricity users. The goal, Sivaram said, is to turn data centers into "good grid citizens" that communities see as assets rather than burdens. What we're watching: Whether regulators actually create the fast lane the coalition wants. Federal regulators in June directed regional grid operators to examine new options for connecting large, flexible power users, providing an opening for the approach AEMA is advocating. Editor's note: Amy Harder is a fellow at the University of Chicago's Institute for Climate and Sustainable Growth, but was not involved in the polling and received no advance access beyond that provided to other journalists. Editor's note: This story has been corrected to note that 76% of Republicans (not 78%) support requiring data center developers to pay for grid upgrades.

events.title: Polymarket’s Next Bet? It Can Also Be a Media Company
events.summary: Every day, a newsletter from the prediction market Polymarket hits my inbox with a subject line that could easily come from any number of politics-focused newspapers or magazines. Recent entries include “Houthis Reveal New Precision Strike Capabilities,” “BREAKING: Trump Unveils Green Energy Beam,” and “World War I, 2.0?” These dispatches are roundups with breathless summaries of the day’s top stories, linking out to corresponding Polymarket markets—yes, this thing will happen; no, it won’t. As far as business news analysis goes, the newsletter is not exactly Bloomberg’s Money Stuff , or even Emily Sundberg’s Feed Me —but it’s recognizably a commercial editorial product, and one that plays an important role in the prediction market ecosystem. The industry is currently embroiled in a series of legal battles over whether prediction markets are financial services (the view held by the markets and the federal government) or gambling platforms (the position of many state authorities and regulators). The fight over what kind of companies these are could end up in the Supreme Court, but in the meantime, both Polymarket and its even-more-popular archrival, Kalshi, have successfully positioned themselves as new media organizations too. For two companies associated with risk, it’s a notably old-school hedge. All kinds of tech startups have launched editorial projects—did you know the alternative dating app Feeld has a surprisingly good magazine?—but the leading prediction markets are entrenching themselves into the mainstream media apparatus in a particularly aggressive way. A recent report noted that they’re integrated into a quarter of the top 20 companies listed in the S&P 500’s Communications Services sector. Polymarket has partnerships with Dow Jones and Substack, while Kalshi has deals with CNN, CNBC, and Fox Corp. None of the agreements facilitate trading. Instead, they’re mainly about data sharing; news outlets want to know what people are putting their money on, and prediction markets are happy to oblige. The deals showcase prediction markets as information channels—places to go to find out about what’s happening. They’ve given Polymarket and Kalshi much-needed boosts in credibility and offered a straightforward introduction to the wider public. Prediction market boosters hype these products as “truth machines,” revealing public sentiment more accurately than polling or traditional reporting; when media outlets decide the odds themselves are newsworthy , they reinforce that message. “Given the forecasting success of the markets, it's clear there is informational value,” says Kalshi spokesperson Jack Such. “And three out of four users don't trade, which suggests the informational use case is popular enough to be taken very seriously.” (Polymarket declined to comment.) Providing data is only a small part of how these companies function as new media entities. On social media, their official accounts post like news outlets, adopting a vernacular that mashes up PopCrave’s frenzied sensibility with Bloomberg’s coverage areas. (The efforts haven’t been wholly reliable: A New York Times analysis earlier this year found that Polymarket’s newsy social accounts have published “false and misleading information.”) Chief executive and founder Shayne Coplan has referred to the company’s partnership with X as “News 2.0.” In 2024, the company hinted at even more expansive ambitions, recruiting for an editor in chief role to lead “content and data journalism” efforts. It never made that hire, although political analyst and media founder Nate Silver came on later that year as an adviser. But on its careers page , the company beckons prospective employees by playing this angle up: “Become the new front page of the internet.” Kalshi is less inclined to describe itself this way. When asked if it considered itself a media company, Such, the spokesperson, tells WIRED that it does not, though the markets themselves have “quasi-media” attributes because they follow the news. “We see ourselves as a financial exchange,” he says. Sure. But why not both? Financial services companies have jumped into the media sector before, most obviously Bloomberg, which initially focused on providing market data and financial analytics before expanding to include journalism products. More recently, the online trading hub Robinhood—now also a Polymarket competitor with its own prediction market offerings—ran a media subsidiary called Sherwood before winding it down earlier this summer. Then there’s Hunterbook, which operates both an investigative outlet called Hunterbook News and a hedge fund that executes trades based on its outlet’s investigations. Polymarket doesn’t have a dedicated subsidiary or editorial arm. But it has launched a weekly podcast called What Are the Odds? in partnership with the podcast network Dear Media.
