events.title: House Democrat pushes global effort on AI rules
events.summary: House Democrats are circulating a letter imploring President Donald Trump to lead an international effort to set global AI rules, according to a copy shared with Semafor. “We strongly urge your administration to lead a coordinated international effort to establish a global framework to guide the development of this technology and a shared vision for AI end-use — engaging our strongest allies, such as the European Union, as well as formidable global competitors, particularly the People’s Republic of China,” Rep. Yassamin Ansari, D-Ariz., writes in the draft of the letter to be sent later this week. It’s unclear which other lawmakers will sign on. The push precedes President Donald Trump’s meeting with Chinese leader Xi Jinping, which will touch on AI. Panic over AI’s capabilities is also rising among lawmakers and the American public. “We must lead with the creation of global rules of the road to prevent the proliferation of uncontrollable highly capable frontier AI,” the letter reads, comparing the push to past US-led efforts on nuclear power and aviation. The US has been very clear about its desire to lead China in AI development, and it’s unlikely that the Trump administration would play any role in international policy decisions about AI that would involve ceding competitive ground. On Sunday, Trump rejected calls by tech leaders for a slowdown in AI development, citing the need for the US to outcompete China. The White House has often opted out of global discussions about AI; last year, White House science adviser Michael Kratsios said at the UN: “We totally reject all efforts by international bodies to assert centralized control and global governance of AI.” It’s still possible the rapid pace of AI development will shift the administration’s approach. Trump’s talks with Xi on AI, and the upcoming UN General Assembly, will present a chance to test whether his administration has altered course at all.

events.title: Republicans’ time crunch: Data centers, sports, crypto
events.summary: The News Some Republicans are hoping they can address voters’ affordability concerns before the election — potentially by passing a data center power bill to demonstrate the party is listening to souring popular sentiment surrounding AI infrastructure. The House is set to take up the bill, called the Ratepayer Protection Act, this week, which will help vulnerable incumbents answer voters’ concerns about data centers. If the Senate takes it up, the bill would help endangered Sen. Jon Husted, R-Ohio. But the body has other priorities: The Senate is scheduled to take up the crypto market structure bill and a huge bipartisan college sports bill as soon as this week. There’s a faction of Republicans who’d rather concentrate on deregulatory rollbacks and addressing AI’s impact on utility bills; Republicans will try and sort it out this week in party meetings. Know More Most Senate denizens expect Tuesday’s crypto bill to fail given the standoff over new ethics rules governing President Donald Trump and his family. The Protect College Sports Act has better prospects and could receive a vote as early as this week. Members of both parties are optimistic about the college sports bill despite Democrats’ filibuster leverage, and one of the bill’s wealthy benefactors is trying to make sure it stays front and center. Saving College Sports, a group founded by Texas Tech University System Board of Regents Chair Cody Campbell, is spending an additional $300,000 on ads between Monday and Tuesday on programs watched closely by lawmakers, including on Fox News, MS NOW and CNN, according to a person familiar with the plans. If the bill advances on the Senate floor, it could take a significant amount of time to process — especially if there’s a protracted amendment fight. That would threaten to eat into the limited three-week work session before the midterm elections, limiting other legislative action; Senate Republicans also wanted to confirm Trump’s judicial nominees and Keith Sonderling, his new pick for Labor secretary. Senate Republicans are also coordinating with the House about deregulatory rollbacks they might be able to accomplish this month. The House is scheduled to take up two California environmental disapproval resolutions this week — members’ last week in town before they break ahead of the midterms. By taking the lead on the data center power bill, House Republicans could provide some political cover for that bill’s sponsor, purple-district Rep. Gabe Evans, R-Colo. The House is also set to vote on a Senate-passed bill named for the late Sen. Lindsey Graham, R-S.C., that would ratchet up pressure on Russia by penalizing its trading partners, though many House Democrats are expected to oppose it because of concerns about handing over more tariff authority to Trump.

events.title: Can Iran replace sea trade with land routes?
events.summary: Iran is shifting trade toward northern ports and land routes as its southern shipping faces a US blockade. Analysts say the corridors can keep essential goods moving, but cannot replace maritime trade. Can land corridors offset the impact of the maritime blockade on Iran ? The US-led maritime blockade targeting Iranian ports has severely disrupted trade through its southern ports, but it is also accelerating a strategy Tehran had discussed for years: moving more commerce through northern ports, railways and land corridors. Economy Minister Ali Madanizadeh, visiting Moscow for talks with Russian officials, said Iran should activate its northern borders and shift a significant share of imports and exports away from the country's southern maritime routes . The idea is straightforward. Iran has seven land neighbors, access to the Caspian Sea and several routes linking it to Russia, Central Asia, Turkey, Iraq, Pakistan and the Caucasus. In theory, that gives Tehran more options than a country dependent on a single maritime gateway. The question is whether those routes have enough capacity to replace what is being lost at sea. Northern routes offer room to expand Alireza Salavati, a London-based political economy commentator, told DW that Iran does have unused capacity. "Iran has more room to maneuver than its dependence on southern ports might suggest,” he said. Iranian authorities said in late 2025 that the country's northern ports had more than 30 million tons of nominal annual capacity, with less than one-third in use. That suggests room for more grain, food and general cargo through the Caspian Sea. Turkey provides another route toward Europe. Rail freight between Iran and Turkey depends partly on train ferries across Lake Van, which carried about 477,000 tons in 2024. To the northeast, Sarakhs and Incheh Borun connect Iran through Turkmenistan toward Central Asia, Russia and potentially China. To the northwest, Astara is part of the International North-South Transport Corridor linking Iran to Azerbaijan and Russia, he said. The Astara freight terminal is designed for 3.5 to 4 million tons a year, but handled only about 345,000 tons in the first five months of 2026. The unfinished Rasht-Astara rail link remains an important bottleneck. For specific goods, these routes matter. Grain from Russia and Kazakhstan, medicines, industrial inputs and regional trade can be redirected more easily than crude oil. Jafar Ghaderi, a member of Iranian parliament's Economic Commission, recently said that 83% of what he described as Iran's 210 million tons of imports had traditionally moved through southern maritime borders, a tremendous volume of goods. "Whenever we are under a maritime blockade, we face problems," hhe said. "How much capacity do our eastern, western and northern corridors actually have?" The cost difference is also large. Majidreza Hariri, head of the Iran-China Chamber of Commerce, said shipping one container from China to Iran through southern ports costs about $3,000 (€2,580), and that moving the same container overland costs roughly $12,000. With around 2 million containers entering through the south annually, Hariri estimated that a prolonged shift to land routes could add about $18 billion to Iran's trading costs. Salavati said the physical arithmetic helps explain why. A 50,000-ton shipload would require around 2,000 truck journeys if each lorry carried 25 tons. Those trucks would then be unavailable for domestic distribution, while longer journeys increase fuel, insurance, warehousing and border costs. Low-value goods are particularly vulnerable because transport expenses account for a larger share of their final price. Umud Shokri, an energy strategist and senior visiting fellow at George Mason University, said Iranian officials are often discussing two different kinds of alternatives. One involves alternative navigation lanes around Hormuz. The other involves shifting trade toward Pakistan, Iraq, Turkey, the Caspian region, Jask and Chabahar. Neither provides a full substitute for southern energy exports . A large crude tanker can carry roughly 1.5 to 2 million barrels. Replicating that volume by road would require thousands of tanker trucks. Rail is more efficient, but still cannot match the cost, speed or scale of maritime transport. Pakistan can help move imports through Karachi, Port Qasim and Gwadar. Iraq can support regional trade and limited fuel flows. Caspian routes can connect Iran to Russia, Kazakhstan and Azerbaijan. But none can replace large-scale crude shipments to Asian buyers. "So the plan is realistic as a resilience strategy, but not as a replacement strategy,” Shokri told DW. How much oil is getting through the Strait of Hormuz? Jask pipeline shows both potential and limits The Goreh-Jask pipeline was built specifically to reduce Iran's dependence on the Strait of Hormuz by moving crude to the Gulf of Oman.

events.title: Citi raised more than $40 billion for Saudi clients this year
events.summary: The Scoop Citigroup has raised more than $40 billion to support Saudi clients so far this year, and increased its direct exposure to the kingdom since the Iran war began, maintaining its bet on the kingdom as a key growth market. The US bank has decided to boost internal exposure limits because Saudi Arabia has demonstrated “strong economic resilience and financial resilience,” Citi’s chief country officer for Saudi Arabia, Fahad Aldeweesh, told Semafor in an interview. Saudi Arabia remains a “high priority market for Citi,” with room to grow despite disruptions caused by more than six months of conflict in the region and Iran’s attempts to shut down shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Under CEO Jane Fraser, Citi has made Saudi Arabia a key part of its growth plans, establishing a regional headquarters in Riyadh last year and aggressively pursuing mandates on deals across initial public offerings, merger and acquisitions, and debt financings. Fraser was named co-chair of the US-Saudi Business Council last year. Citi also acted as one of the global coordinators on Saudi Arabia’s $3.25 billion islamic bond sale earlier this month, and is reportedly advising Aramco on a potential sale of a stake in its oil export and storage terminals. “It’s very helpful for our efforts on the ground to support clients here at this time and also to show confidence in the prospects of the country region during this period,” Aldeweesh said, declining to comment on specific transactions. Know More Citi has been working on boosting its Saudi footprint for several years. Although it first entered the kingdom in 1955 when it was the first US bank to operate there, it sold a stake in one of Saudi’s largest banks in 2004, ending its on-the-ground presence. It returned in 2017 with an investment banking license as Crown Prince Mohammed Bin Salman embarked on an economic overhaul that attracted Wall Street’s biggest names, tempted by fees on government debt sales, Aramco’s IPO, and international acquisitions by the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. Saudi Arabia is expected to be a strong driver for investment banking deals in coming years as it sells more debt and seeks foreign investors. Public Investment Fund has made attracting third-party capital to help fund its economic transformation projects as a pillar of its new five-year strategy and recently sent executives to New York to drum up interest from potential investors, Semafor reported last week. Courtesy of Citi International private equity and infrastructure investors are showing greater interest in the kingdom, Aldeweesh said. “We see them actively looking for opportunities and also hoping additional deal flow would be made available to them,” he said. Foreign stock market investors have added $3 billion to their Saudi holdings since the start of the year, he added, boosting Citi’s trading and custody business. Citi has a “strong” transaction pipeline in the works and is optimistic that IPO activity will pick up in coming months, Aldeweesh added. The bank employs around 35 staff in Saudi Arabia and plans to keep hiring, he said, declining to specify how many will be recruited. Notable Citi opened its regional headquarters in Riyadh last year, signalling a commitment from the US bank to join peers seeking to establish a stronger foothold with the government and PIF, Bloomberg reported in October.

events.title: Inside the US Treasury secretary’s tense relationship with financial media
events.summary: The Scoop Last September, Bloomberg News Editor-in-Chief John Micklethwait got a call from US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent. The secretary had been a regular on Bloomberg’s TV programming and in its reporting for years, first as the founder of a hedge fund, and increasingly as he rose in Donald Trump’s circle to become the most powerful financial official in the now-president’s Cabinet. He was furious that Bloomberg reporters Anthony Cormier and Zachary Mider planned to report that Bessent had agreed to simultaneously occupy two different houses as his “principal residence,” two people familiar with the exchange told Semafor — just as Trump was trying to use the same rationale to justify firing Federal Reserve Governor Lisa Cook. During the conversation, Bessent told Micklethwait that if Bloomberg went ahead with a piece whose accuracy he heatedly disputed the financial news giant could expect different treatment from the Treasury Department — including no more appearances by the Treasury secretary, a coveted TV guest. Bessent’s team also wanted more time to provide further documentation. Bloomberg published the article anyway . But in the year since, Bessent has followed through on his threat. The secretary stopped appearing on Bloomberg Television. Some of its reporters privately complain that they no longer receive certain press releases with key financial information. Bloomberg and Wall Street Journal journalists were also denied credentials to join Bessent at a G20 meeting of financial leaders in Asheville, North Carolina, earlier this month; a Times reporter was also denied credentials, though another was included among some 300 reporters credentialed. A spokesperson for Bloomberg declined to comment. Bessent appears regularly on Sunday morning interview shows, and doesn’t shirk adversarial interviews. But his rift with Bloomberg is part of a tense and distant relationship between the powerful Cabinet secretary and the press corps that covers him, which includes both high-profile finance reporters and the typically lower-key in-house Treasury press. As high interest rates remain front-page news — and so-called bond vigilantes test Treasury’s credibility — critical headlines in financial and business publications have frustrated a secretary who didn’t spend his career seeking the public eye, and doesn’t seem to think all those who cover him are up to the job. In public over the last several weeks, Bessent has railed against the Financial Times for reporting that he had discussed tightening Treasury’s oversight of the Federal Reserve by adopting elements of the Bank of England’s model, describing the story as “tabloid trash for market participants” and calling the reporters “pathetic” and “mendacious.” He’s called out Nick Timiraos, the Journal’s well-regarded chief economic correspondent, dubbing him one of the “stenographers posing as journalists” over what Bessent characterized as weak reporting on monetary policy. And in private, Bessent has complained personally to reporters and editors about coverage, and iced out journalists he and his team feel have been unfair. The New York Times first reported earlier this month that certain reporters from the Times, Journal, and Bloomberg had not received press credentials to cover the G20 event. Know More The cadre of reporters devoted full-time to Treasury have largely avoided the big Trump-era confrontations that have defined the White House and Pentagon beats. The group — which includes beat reporters from The Wall Street Journal, The New York Times, Bloomberg, the Financial Times, and the wire services — is more used to choreographed exchanges with officials than heated on-camera back-and-forths. During Trump’s 2024 campaign, Bessent was broadly a helpful surrogate to many economic policy reporters, a figure with serious Wall Street credentials who could translate the then-former president’s occasionally hazy vision for the economy into more concrete policy. But upon taking office, the Treasury secretary showed he was going to have a different relationship with the press. When Bessent traveled to Ukraine in February 2025, he did not do it with most of the normal Treasury beat reporters in tow. One of the few members of the media who did go along was Jack Posobiec, the Pizzagate figure turned conservative influencer. That was the first sign that things would be different from Trump’s first term, when then-Treasury Secretary Steve Mnuchin regularly brought the press along on the department’s plane, fielding on- and off-the-record questions about fiscal policy during flights (though he stopped after Mnuchin’s use of a private government jet became a focal point of media coverage). But Mnuchin’s friendlier media strategy has not aged particularly well within Trump’s MAGA circle. When Semafor brought up Mnuchin’s friendly relationship to the press compared to Bessent’s recent criticism, one Trump-world figure bluntly told me, “Notice that he’s not in the job this time around.” Now, the press corps does not travel with the secretary, a frustration for journalists, though a Treasury insider said it was the result of plane retrofitting and assignment logistics, forcing journalists and some senior staff to fly commercial. Reporters’ literal movements within Treasury are also becoming more restricted. Earlier this year, a draft of a letter to communications officials Alexandra Preate and Elliott Hulse circulated among journalists requesting guidance on the department’s policies for issuing hard passes, which allow journalists to enter and move within the building, and use a designated press area for work. The letter noted that while some reporters had been told hard passes would be restored when the department brought in a new public affairs officer, it also noted that the department had told some journalists that it would not issue them hard passes at all. “Press access to the Treasury building is essential to helping reporters give thorough and accurate information to the widest possible audience,” the letter said. The letter circulated through the press corps, but ultimately was not sent. A Treasury source downplayed the hard pass restrictions, noting that there had been little demand, and said the department had simply kept a policy in place implemented during the Biden administration’s COVID pandemic-era restrictions. (A former Biden administration official said Treasury did credential reporters post-pandemic.) The Treasury source also cited tightened Secret Service rules, which include requiring non-Americans to travel within the buildings with an escort. Frustrations with the mainstream media have meanwhile driven Bessent more towards friendly ideological territory; in recent days, he’s made time for the news streaming channel Right Side Broadcasting, Fox News, and Steve Bannon’s show. events.title: Dems' primary plan gives Native Americans more power
events.summary: The 2028 race for the White House will give new political clout to a long-overlooked constituency: Native American voters. Driving the news: New Mexico now holds an influential early spot as one of the first states to vote in the Democratic primary — on Feb. 15, 2028. That's put Native Americans , who make up about 12% of the state, in position to wield more influence in the presidential race than ever before. In recent Democratic primaries, New Mexico typically has voted late in the season, in June. States that held the earliest primaries had much smaller Native populations. Now potential presidential campaigns are scrambling to adjust to the 2028 lineup, calling Native leaders to learn about Indigenous power players and the dynamics of tribal governments, Democratic operatives tell Axios. Zoom in: Any presidential candidate who wants to win New Mexico is "going to have to listen to tribes," warned Deb Haaland, the former U.S. interior secretary who made history in 2021 when she became the first Native American to head a cabinet agency. "We could be a large part in who that nominee is." Native leaders and their allies say that will force presidential candidates to engage closely with tribal governments and pay attention to issues such as tribal sovereignty, land and water rights, and rural infrastructure. Several potential 2028 contenders are already taking notes. Isaac Dakota Casados, a New Mexico Democratic consultant and Navajo Nation member, told us his phone has been ringing off the hook as presidential campaigns-in-waiting look to learn more about Native voters. "They're really trying to figure out how the Native American demographic plays into this larger picture," he said. "I think they're used to speaking to Hispanic and Latino populations within their states. This is a very unique variable that's very different to them." Casados said Illinois Gov. JB Pritzker acknowledged to him that he's "really gotta learn" about tribal leadership, while New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker was "fascinated" by New Mexico's myriad tribal cultures in a recent conversation. Kalyn Free, a Choctaw Nation citizen who's on the Democratic National Committee's powerful rules and bylaws committee, also said she's been getting outreach from presidential hopefuls and their teams. The jockeying among 2028ers to win Native American voters could help elevate new power brokers in the Indigenous community. Tribal governments will likely be courted for endorsements. Haaland, a member of the Laguna Pueblo, is uniquely poised to become a sought-after validator for 2028 candidates in Indian country: She's running for governor of New Mexico this year. Some potential 2028 contenders already appear to be wooing Haaland. She met recently with Booker and is rallying with former Transportation Secretary Pete Buttigieg this weekend. Pritzker helped raise money for Haaland at an event in New Mexico this month. Haaland told us she talked with Pritzker about her efforts to investigate the troubled legacy of federal Indian boarding schools and President Trump's slashing of protections for Native American sacred sites. Asked if she would endorse a candidate in the 2028 primary, Haaland said: "I would wait to see." Zoom out: New Mexico has the nation's third-largest share of people who identify as American Indian or Alaska Native, and it includes 23 federally recognized tribes. When New Mexico votes in the presidential primary, the race will probably have been narrowed to two or three candidates — giving the state an oversized say in helping pick the party's nominee, Democratic strategists say. Native leaders say their community's voters don't easily map onto the party's progressive-vs.-moderate divide, and stressed that the community isn't a monolith in general elections, either. In the 2016 Democratic primary, Hillary Clinton won some states with significant Native populations, such as New Mexico and Arizona — but Bernie Sanders carried others, such as Alaska and Montana. In 2024's general election, some Native voters across the country — who polls suggested had been hit particularly hard by inflation — shifted toward Trump. What's next: Democrats hope that by putting New Mexico early in the primary lineup, they'll learn how to better win Native Americans and reverse that trend. "These votes really matter," said New Mexico Gov. Michelle Lujan Grisham (D), noting that Native voters have been the margin of difference for presidential candidates in some battlegrounds. "We credit the Navajo Nation vote to getting Biden over the finish line in Arizona" in 2020. Flashback: This year Native American leaders lobbied the Democratic National Committee to add New Mexico to the early primary calendar. In February, the All Pueblo Council of Governors passed a resolution that said doing so would "transform the relationship between presidential candidates and Pueblo peoples," whereas the old lineup had been "effectively silencing" Native voices. Axios' Russell Contreras contributed reporting.
